speaker: Moses Kagan
title: Repositioning 80 Apartment Buildings with Moses Kagan
question: In urban multifamily real estate repositioning, how do operators generate outsized returns in the $2.5 million to $10 million building segment despite its small deal sizes?
guest: The first thing to understand is that Los Angeles multifamily real estate is extremely attractive, and as you climb up in asset size, those buildings attract a lot of interest from players who have cheap capital, like pension fund money. So if you're trying to generate supernormal returns, it made sense to us to focus on sub-institutional scale deals—in the range of $2.5 million on the low end up to around $10 million on the high end. Those deals are a little bit more complicated and capital-intensive than what a standard retail buyer, like a dentist wanting to buy a building, would do, but they're also way smaller than what an institutional real estate private equity fund would want to do. The result is you can generate supernormal returns. The downside is it's a very inefficient way to place capital—doing a $2.5 million deal here and a $5 million deal there takes a long time to deploy material capital. To square that circle, you figure out how to do a lot of projects at once. We've evolved and trained employees to run a whole bunch of deals in parallel—we're doing nine right now and have done as many as 20 at a time.

Operators in this segment profit mainly from an inefficiency gap: buildings priced at $2.5–10 million are too large for most individual investors yet too small for institutions, whose overhead and capital-deployment minimums make such deals uneconomical. That thin competition lets skilled buyers acquire at higher cap rates, often off-market, from long-time "mom-and-pop" owners who have under-managed the asset, leaving rents below market, deferred maintenance, and bloated expenses.

Returns then come from forced appreciation. Operators renovate units and common areas, add amenities and revenue lines (laundry, parking, storage, utility bill-backs), and install professional management to cut costs and vacancy. Because value equals net operating income divided by cap rate, each dollar of added income creates many dollars of value.

Scale is solved by aggregation: clustering many small buildings in the same neighborhoods to share management, maintenance crews, and purchasing. The stabilized portfolio can then be refinanced to recycle equity or sold to an institutional buyer at a lower cap rate, capturing a portfolio premium on top of the property-level gains. Moderate leverage amplifies the result.
